opus-5.5.text:
I think pre-training is what made reinforcement learning finally work in a general way. For a long time, people in RL focused on the algorithm, things like better policy gradients or better value functions, and on the environment, like Atari, Go, or MuJoCo. The third ingredient, priors, was underrated. It turns out priors might be the most important part, and you get them from pre-training.

Here's an example. Imagine you put an RL agent from five or ten years ago into a text adventure game or a web browser. The action space is basically infinite: you can type any sentence or click anywhere. If you start from scratch with random exploration, you will almost never stumble onto something meaningful, because the reward is too sparse. A language model that has read the internet already knows what a "door" is, what "search" means, roughly how a website works, and how people solve problems. So exploration becomes structured. You aren't sampling random tokens. You're sampling plausible thoughts and plausible actions.

Reasoning matters a lot here too. One thing we found working on agents like ReAct is that when you let the model think before it acts, thinking itself becomes a kind of action. It doesn't change the external world, but it changes the model's own context. In classical RL, adding an action like "think" would seem useless, because it has infinitely many possibilities and no direct reward. With language priors, thinking generalizes. The model can reason about a new environment it has never seen before and make a sensible decision. That's why RL on top of language models can transfer across tasks in a way earlier RL couldn't.

So I'd say pre-training gives you the foundation: knowledge of the world, language as a general interface, and the ability to reason. RL then turns that potential into goal-directed behavior. In the first half of AI, people mostly trained better models and climbed benchmarks. Now that the recipe of pre-training, reasoning, and RL basically works, the question shifts. It becomes less "can we solve this task" and more "what tasks should we define, and how do we evaluate real usefulness." That's what I think of as the second half.

r001.rationale: The response presents pre-training and RL as ingredients that support reasoning and goal-directed behavior, but it does not clearly distinguish agents as the desired outcome from those technologies.

r002.rationale: It explains that from-scratch exploration in text adventures or browsers is unlikely to find meaningful actions because rewards are sparse, while pre-training supplies priors that structure exploration.

r003.rationale: It says random exploration would almost never find something meaningful, but does not clearly frame this as prohibitive sample requirements despite theoretical solvability.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is that pre-training is what makes reinforcement learning finally work at scale, and that's not a small thing, because RL has been around for decades and for most of that time it didn't really work outside of games.

If you look back at the classic RL story, Atari, Go, Dota, StarCraft, those were all incredible results, but they shared a weakness. Every one of them started from a randomly initialized network and learned everything from scratch inside one environment. That meant you needed an enormous number of samples, you needed a very clean reward signal, and whatever the agent learned didn't transfer anywhere. The policy that played Go could not do anything else. So RL was powerful but brittle, and it was basically confined to environments where you could simulate forever and the reward was obvious.

Pre-training changes the starting point. Instead of a random policy, you begin with a model that already has a huge amount of prior knowledge about the world, about language, about how to reason, about what tasks even look like. And I think the key word there is prior. When I was working on ReAct and later on things like WebShop and SWE-bench, the thing that struck me was that a language model, with zero RL, could already take reasonable actions in a new environment just because of what it absorbed in pre-training. It knew what a shopping website was, it knew what a Python traceback meant. That's a prior that no amount of Atari RL could give you.

So when you then apply RL on top, you're not teaching the model what a task is. You're teaching it how to do the task well, how to explore, how to recover from mistakes, how to decide when to think more. The exploration problem, which is the thing that killed RL in most real settings, becomes tractable because the model's initial guesses are already close to sensible. You're searching in a much smaller, much more meaningful space.

And there's a second piece that I think people underrate. Pre-training also gives you generalization across environments. In the old RL era, each environment was its own universe. Now, because the agent is a language model, the same model can act in a browser, in a terminal, in a code repository, in a conversation. Language is the common interface. That means RL signal you collect in one domain actually improves behavior in another, and that's what lets you even talk about a general agent rather than a hundred narrow ones.

So the way I'd frame it: pre-training solved the prior and the generalization, and RL solves the decision making. Neither one alone gets you to agents. Pre-training alone gives you something that knows a lot but can't reliably act over long horizons or learn from the consequences of its actions. RL alone gives you something that can optimize but doesn't know anything. Put them together and you get a system that starts out knowing the world and then learns from experience in it. That combination is really what made the current wave of agents possible, and I think it also tells you where the bottleneck has moved. It's less about the model now and more about the environments and the rewards we can give it.

r001.rationale: It presents pre-training and RL as complementary technologies, assigns each a role, and says their combination makes agents possible.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training supplies useful prior knowledge that makes RL work at scale, including in browser and code environments.

r003.rationale: It says learning from scratch needs enormous samples and limits RL to settings that can be simulated extensively, but does not explain that this can make RL infeasible even when solving the environment is theoretically possible.

astra-6.text:
I think pre-training provides the foundation that makes reinforcement learning useful. If you start with a randomly initialized model, it’s very hard to learn a complex task through trial and error. The model may never do anything meaningful enough to receive a positive reward. Pre-training gives it language, knowledge, and a broad repertoire of behaviors, so exploration starts from a much better place.

For agents, this is especially important because the action space is so broad. An action might be writing code, using a tool, or asking a question. Pre-training gives the model some understanding of what those actions mean and when they might be useful. Reinforcement learning can then improve how it chooses and sequences them through feedback from the environment.

But knowing how people describe a task is different from being able to complete it. An agent has to act, observe the result, and recover when something goes wrong. So I see pre-training as giving us a very strong starting point, while reinforcement learning helps turn that broad capability into behavior that reliably achieves a goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training and reinforcement learning as useful for building agents, but does not clearly distinguish agents as the desired outcome from those methods as technologies.

r002.rationale: It calls pre-training the foundation that makes reinforcement learning useful and explains why learning complex tasks through trial and error from random initialization is impractical; its agent examples involve language, code, and tools.

r003.rationale: It says learning from random initialization is very hard, but does not identify prohibitive sample requirements or distinguish practical infeasibility from theoretical possibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pre-training gives reinforcement learning a very good starting point. If you ask an agent to learn everything from scratch through trial and error, the space is enormous. It has to learn language, acquire knowledge, understand the environment, and discover useful actions before it can even begin solving the task you care about.

With pre-training, a lot of that is already there. The model has learned patterns of reasoning, code, and descriptions of how people solve problems. So reinforcement learning can work with an existing repertoire of behaviors: which action should I take here, when should I use a tool, and how should I adjust after receiving feedback?

But knowing how to describe an action is different from reliably taking it. A model might generate a convincing plan without being able to execute that plan over many steps. That’s where interaction becomes important. The agent takes an action, observes what actually happened, and continues. Reinforcement learning can help turn those capabilities into behavior that succeeds in an environment.

So I see pre-training and reinforcement learning as complementary. Pre-training makes a broad range of useful behavior possible; reinforcement learning helps the model discover how to use that capability to achieve a goal.

r001.rationale: The response calls pre-training and reinforcement learning complementary and discusses agents, but does not distinguish agents as the desired outcome from the two methods as technologies.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training gives reinforcement learning a good starting point, but does not identify it as a practical prerequisite specifically in text-based environments.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from scratch as requiring work across an enormous space, but does not explain prohibitive sample requirements or distinguish practical infeasibility from theoretical possibility.
